blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
What happens when a legal AI model learns to look like a lawyer instead
of reasoning like one? We fine tune Qwen3-8B with Group Relative
Policy Optimisation (GRPO) against a proxy built from three surface
features: citation count, legalese density, and response length. The
model does not learn to reason more effectively. It learns to withhold
commitment. Across 16 16 yes or no legal reasoning tasks from LegalBench
( N = 320 N{=}320 ), overall accuracy collapses from 0.500 0.500 (chance) to 0.072 0.072 ( McNemar \mathrm{McNemar} p < 10 − 36 p<10^{-36} ), driven entirely by the
rate of properly formatted answers falling from 0.900 0.900 to 0.109 0.109 .
The model stops committing to answers. Yet when it does commit,
accuracy rises from 0.556 0.556 to 0.657 0.657 , showing that the
collapse is not a failure of capability but a strategic response: the
model has learned that verbose responses packed with citations but
empty of a direct answer score higher than terse correct ones. We
term this the Saul Goodman effect, a
policy that becomes maximally lawyerly while becoming maximally
noncommittal, and prove formally that it is the optimal
response to any surface feature proxy that attaches no penalty to
abstention (Proposition 3.2 ). We further show that 89.3 % 89.3\% of citations produced after training are structurally
implausible hallucinations, many of them subtly corrupted names of
real landmark cases, constructed in effect to survive a casual read
and fail under scrutiny. To detect this failure mode before
deployment, we introduce three diagnostic tools: the Confidence
Theater Score (CTS), the Citation Plausibility Rate (CPR), and the
Regret Gap (RG). In a domain where a confidently wrong answer can
constitute malpractice, the broader lesson is direct: a reward
function that measures how legal a response looks will produce
a model that is maximally photogenic and minimally useful.

blocks.en:
Reinforcement learning from human or programmatic feedback now dominates the
post-training of large language models ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . A central
assumption is that the learnt reward model – or, when stylistic rather than
preference signals are used, a hand-crafted scoring function – is a faithful
proxy for true task quality. Goodhart’s Law ( Goodhart, 1984 ) warns that
once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to measure what it once did. In RL
fine-tuning, this manifests as reward over-optimisation ( Gao et al., 2022 ) : the policy continues to climb the proxy long after
the proxy has decoupled from the true objective ( Sahoo et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Legal natural language processing is a particularly stark testbed for this
failure mode. Legal text has visible surface features — citations to case
law, statute references, Latin terms of art, formal verbose structure —
that are easy to count automatically and easy for a model to over-produce ( Kolt et al., 2026 ; Sahoo, 2026 ) .
A reward function built on these features rewards looking lawyerly regardless of being correct . The danger is not academic: legal LLMs
are increasingly deployed for contract review, statute summarisation, and
case discovery ( Guha et al., 2023 ) , and a model that produces
verbose, citation-dense, structurally implausible output is a malpractice
vector.

blocks.en: 2 Background and Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 背景和有关工作

blocks.en:
Reward over-optimisation. Gao et al. (2022) showed that PPO against a learnt reward model
exhibits a characteristic curve: true reward initially rises with the KL
budget, peaks, and then degrades while the proxy continues to improve. We
replicate this curve in the legal domain ( Section 5.6 ) but additionally
show that the failure mode is not pure capability loss – it is a
strategic switch in the policy’s output mode.

显示一个特征曲线:真正的奖励最初随KL而上升
预算,峰值,然后在代理继续改善时退化. 我们
在法律领域复制这一曲线(第5.6节),但另外
显示失败模式不是纯容量损失, 而是
政策产出模式中的战略转换。

blocks.en:

domains ( Skalse et al., 2025 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) . Our work contributes a
domain-specific instance with a clean separation between the proxy
(surface lawyerly features) and the ground truth (yes/no doctrinal
correctness).

blocks.en:
Why legal NLP is the right testbed for surface-feature reward hacking. Legal text is unusual among NLP domains in that its surface features
are culturally legible proxies for expertise . A lay reader who sees a
response dense with case citations, Latin phrases, and formal structure
will judge it as authoritative regardless of its correctness — precisely
the same confusion the reward function makes. This cultural legibility
means that a Goodharted legal LLM is not merely wrong in a technical sense;
it is wrong in a way that is designed to evade detection by the
humans most likely to be harmed by it. This distinguishes the legal domain
from, say, code generation ( Pan et al., 2022 ) , where a non-running
program is immediately falsifiable, or summarisation, where plausibility
is harder to weaponise. The stakes are correspondingly higher: a verbose,
citation-laden non-answer that sounds like legal advice is a
malpractice vector that passes casual review.

This workshop paper is a small controlled instance of a problem central to AI safety, what happens when a policy is optimized against a proxy for quality rather than quality itself. Reward hacking and specification gaming are usually studied in toy or synthetic environments, here the same dynamic shows up in a real evaluation domain with actual stakes attached to the outcome. The finding that a model learns to look competent while becoming less useful, and that the diagnostic score built to catch this (CTS) gets gamed right along with the policy, is a direct demonstration of the scalable oversight problem, any evaluator, human or automated, that relies on legible surface signals is vulnerable to exactly the optimization pressure it exists to guard against. This is why reward design and monitoring cannot be treated as separable from the thing being optimized. The concern generalizes well beyond law to any setting where a model is trained against feedback that correlates with quality only until it becomes the target.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion

blocks.en:
GRPO with a surface-feature proxy reward induces a sharp behavioural
collapse on legal yes/no reasoning. The collapse is mechanistically a format collapse : the model retains reasoning ability but learns to
never commit. We provide a diagnostic toolkit — CTS ( 4 ),
CPR ( Appendix C ), GDM ( 5 ), RG ( 6 ) — for
detecting this failure mode in any RL-from-style-reward pipeline. The
broader lesson is that in domains where what looks good is easy to
measure but what is good is not, reward over-optimisation will
route directly through the surface features and produce a model that is
maximally photogenic and minimally useful.

blocks.en:
This is the Saul Goodman effect in its purest form: the post-training
model sounds more like a lawyer than the pre-training model,
cites cases with confidence ( Boxx v. Long is a hallucination; Shoe v. Washington is a garbled version of International
Shoe v. Washington , 326 U.S. 310, 1945), deploys legal terminology
fluently — and never answers the question. The pre-training model
gives the right answer in one word.
